title: git add -i: the menu almost nobody opens
summary: Behind `git add -p` there is a whole interactive mode: status, update, revert, add-untracked, patch and diff. Walk the menu, stage by number, and unstage without remembering a single flag.
mental_model: `add -i` is a menu over the index. Each entry maps to a command you already know — update is `git add`, revert is `git restore --staged`, patch is `git add -p` — with a file picker in front of it.

steps.title: Open the menu and read it
steps.why: Option 1 prints a table of every changed file with its staged and unstaged line counts. The eight commands are the whole feature — `add -p` is just option 5 with the picker skipped.
steps.expect: A status table, the command list, and 'Bye.' when q quits.

verify.label: the interactive menu is available
verify.hint: note the menu prints [s]tatus, not status — the bracket is in the output

steps.title: Stage one file by number
steps.why: `2` is update. It lists the files, you type a number, then a blank line confirms the selection. No paths typed, no tab completion needed — this is why it beats `git add` on a repository with long paths.
steps.expect: alerts.py staged; the other two still unstaged.

verify.label: exactly one file was staged from the menu
verify.hint: 2 (update), then the file's number, then a blank line

steps.title: Stage a range
steps.why: The picker takes ranges and multiple selections: `1-2`, or `1 3`, or `*` for everything. On a twenty-file change this is dramatically faster than typing paths.
steps.expect: Both remaining tracked files staged in one selection.

verify.label: a range selection staged the rest

steps.title: Revert one back out
steps.why: `3` is revert, which unstages — the menu's name for `git restore --staged`. Note it works from the same numbered list, so you never have to think about which flag unstages what.
steps.expect: One file moved back to the unstaged column, its edit intact.

steps.title: Add an untracked file without typing its name
steps.why: `4` lists only untracked files. It is the safe way to add new files on a repository with build output lying around — you pick from a list rather than firing `git add -A` and hoping.
steps.expect: README.md staged; scratch.md still untracked because you did not select it.

verify.label: an untracked file was added from the menu
…and the one you did not pick stayed untracked

steps.title: Review what you have assembled
steps.why: `6` is diff, and it shows the STAGED changes against HEAD — the same thing as `git diff --cached`. Reviewing here, inside the menu, is the habit that stops half-staged commits.
steps.expect: The diff of everything currently staged.

steps.title: Drop into patch mode from the menu
steps.why: `5` is patch — the hunk-by-hunk picker you know as `git add -p`, reached with a file selector in front of it. Same keys once you are in: y, n, s to split, e to edit, q to quit.
steps.expect: One file's hunk staged through the patch picker, everything else unstaged again.

verify.label: patch mode staged a single file's hunk
verify.hint: 5 (patch), pick a file, then y to stage the hunk

steps.title: Commit what you chose
steps.why: Nothing about the menu changes what a commit is. It is a faster way to build the index, and the index is what gets committed — as always.

verify.label: the commit contains exactly what you selected
the scratch file was never committed
the commit was assembled through the interactive menu
verify.hint: git add -i, then 5 for patch mode

verify.label: the scratch file stayed untracked throughout
verify.hint: option 4 lists untracked files so you can pick rather than sweep

verify.label: one new commit on top of the setup
the changes you deliberately left out are still in the working tree

pitfalls: `update` stages and `revert` unstages — the names come from the index's point of view, not the working tree's. `revert` here has nothing to do with `git revert`.
A blank line confirms your selection; typing `q` before it discards the selection silently.
`add -i` shows only tracked files under update and revert. New files appear solely under option 4 — the same split that catches people out with `git commit -a`.
`git add -p` is the same code path with the picker skipped. If you only ever want hunks, skip the menu.
The menu is not scriptable and reads stdin, so it hangs in a CI job. Use the plumbing commands in scripts.
cheatsheet: staged and unstaged line counts per file
pick new files from a list
the picker takes ranges, lists and everything
